answer:
**Short answer:** You can't end the lease on your own just because you're transferring schools. The manager is also overstating things when they say you owe rent through July "no matter what."

**What your lease says.** Your lease runs from August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026 (§3). Nothing in it gives you a right to end early. It has no early-termination fee and no liquidated-damages clause. It says it is "the whole agreement" and can be changed only in a signed writing (§10). The manager's email doesn't change the lease.

**What the statute says.** If you leave early, Fla. Stat. §83.595 gives the landlord a choice of remedies:
- **(1) End the lease.** The landlord retakes possession for its own account, and you owe nothing further.
- **(2) Relet for your account.** The landlord retakes possession and relets the unit. It must try in good faith to relet, and any rent it collects is deducted from what you owe. You owe only the difference.
- **(3) Do nothing.** The landlord stands by and holds you liable for the rent as it comes due. This is the manager's position, and the statute allows it.
- **(4) Charge an early-termination fee.** This is allowed only if you signed a separate addendum agreeing to a fee of no more than 2 months' rent, with no more than 60 days' notice required. The addendum must be signed when the lease was made.

**How this applies to you.** The manager can lawfully choose option (3), so you could owe rent through July. That isn't guaranteed, though. If the landlord retakes the unit and relets it, option (2) lowers what you owe. If it ends the lease, you owe nothing further. The 2-month fee cap under option (4) would apply only if you signed a separate addendum. I don't see one in the lease I have.

I haven't seen anything suggesting you qualify for the military-service early-termination rule in §83.682, so I'm not treating it as applying.

**One thing I need from you:** did you sign any separate addendum or paper about an early-termination fee or liquidated damages when you signed the lease?

answer:
Thursday passing with no repair and no AC means the landlord has missed his own promise. Whether you can end the lease over it depends on three things.

**1. Is the AC his legal duty? This is unsettled on what I have.**
- The statute's list of specific duties for apartments names "heat during winter," not cooling (§ 83.51(2)(a)5). It does not name AC.
- His broader duty is to "comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (§ 83.51(1)(a)).
- Your lease says nothing about AC or repairs. It covers rent, deposit, move-out, notices, and holding over.
- Whether a Gainesville or Alachua County code requires working cooling is outside what I can check here. If one does, his failure is a statutory violation. If none does, the statute may not require him to fix it, and you would have no clear right under § 83.56(1). You would then be relying on his promise to repair, which isn't a lease term.

**2. Your texts don't start the 7-day clock.**
- To end the lease, you must deliver a written notice that "specif[ies] the noncompliance" and states that you intend to terminate because of it. If he has not fixed the problem "within 7 days after delivery," you may terminate (§ 83.56(1)).
- Your texts told him the AC was broken, but they did not say you intend to terminate.
- Lease § 7 says written notices to the landlord are delivered "by hand" to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street or sent there "by certified mail." A text is neither.
- The statute allows delivery by mailing, delivering a true copy, or e-mail under § 83.505 (§ 83.56(4)). It also says the notice requirements "may not be waived in the rental agreement."
- Whether the lease's delivery rule or the statute's wider rule controls is open. Hand delivery or certified mail to Suite A satisfies both readings.

**3. Keep paying rent.**
- The statute does not let you withhold rent on your own because of this problem.
- If you pay rent knowing about his noncompliance, you may waive the right to terminate over that violation (§ 83.56(5)(a)).
- A rent reduction under § 83.56(1)(b) applies only when the failure is "due to causes beyond the control of the landlord" and he keeps making "every reasonable effort." Nothing you've told me suggests that.

Do you want to end the lease and move out, or stay and push him to fix the AC?

**What to do:** Object in writing to the $500 deduction. Do it soon, because the objection window is short.

**Why:**
- **The landlord's notice may be on time.** The landlord has 30 days after the rental agreement ends to send a notice of a claim (83.49(3)(a)). I counted from your lease end date and from your move-out date. Both 30-day periods are still running today, 2026-08-20. They end 2026-08-30 and 2026-08-29. So you can't count on getting the whole deposit back because the notice was late. That route needs the 30 days to pass with no proper notice.
- **You have 15 days to object.** If you don't object within 15 days after you receive the notice, the landlord may deduct the claim and must send you the balance. That is 83.49(3)(b). Not objecting does not give up your right to sue later for a refund (83.49(3)(b)).
- **Your deadline isn't set yet.** I can only count 15 days from your receipt date once you confirm that date. I've noted it as today, 2026-08-20, and you need to confirm it in the sidebar. Until then, treat the deadline as close.

**How to object:**
- The statute's form of notice says your objection must be sent to the landlord's address. Use the address in the letter.
- Your lease says written notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address (lease §7). Following that is the safest way. Keep proof that you delivered or mailed it.
- Say you object to the $500 claim and why. Lease §6 says to leave the apartment "clean and empty." It doesn't say anything about carpet cleaning fees or what counts as a charge. The statute doesn't say what a landlord may deduct for either. If you think the carpet was only worn from ordinary use, or that you left it clean, say so.

**What isn't settled:**
- The statute requires the notice to come by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum (83.49(3)(a), 83.505(1)). Your lease says you did not agree to e-mail notices (lease §8).
- If the letter came some other way, there are two readings. One is that it isn't the required notice, so the landlord loses the claim and owes the full deposit. The other is that a notice you actually received in time is enough, because 83.505(6) "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." Either way, objecting costs you nothing and protects you.

**Court costs:** If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee (83.49(3)(c)).

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

answer:
**Short answer:** Your lease doesn't give you a right to end it early, and the manager can hold you to rent through July. That is not "no matter what," though. The amount can drop if the landlord re-rents the apartment.

**What your lease says:** It runs "August 1, 2025" to "July 31, 2026" (§3), and it has no early-termination clause or fee. The only way out it mentions is staying past July with consent (§9). It also says it "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant" (§10). So the manager doesn't have to agree to let you out.

**What the statute says:** Once you surrender or abandon the apartment, Fla. Stat. §83.595 gives the landlord four choices:
- **§83.595(1):** end the lease and retake the apartment for their own account, which ends your liability.
- **§83.595(2):** retake the apartment for your account. You then owe only the difference between your rent and what the landlord gets from re-renting. The landlord must make a good-faith effort to relet, using at least the same efforts they use for similar units.
- **§83.595(3):** "stand by and do nothing," holding you liable for the rent as it comes due.
- **§83.595(4):** charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee.

**How that applies to you:**
- **The manager's position:** "Rent through July" matches option (3), and that choice is the landlord's. If they stand by, you owe rent monthly as it comes due.
- **The fee option:** Option (4) is unavailable on what I can see. It requires a separate signed addendum, and your lease shows none. Even then, the fee could not exceed 2 months' rent.
- **Where it's unsettled:** I can't tell you the landlord has to re-rent. Option (2) applies only if the landlord retakes possession for your account. A landlord who says they will stand by and collect rent is arguably choosing option (3). Whether the landlord is held to that choice if they later re-rent is not settled by the text. If they do re-rent, the rent they receive should reduce what you owe.
- **If you stay:** Moving out does not end your rent obligation. If you leave, you would still be liable under whichever option the landlord uses.

Did you sign any separate addendum about an early termination fee or liquidated damages when you signed the lease?

answer:
Nobody coming Thursday doesn't fit the landlord's promise. Whether it breaks the law depends on a point I can't confirm yet. Your AC has now been out for 7 days, counted from April 11.

**Is the landlord legally required to fix the AC?**
- **The statute.** Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)5 lists "heat during winter, running water, and hot water." It doesn't list air conditioning.
- **Local codes.** § 83.51(1)(a) separately requires the landlord to "comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes." If Gainesville's or Alachua County's housing code requires working cooling, the AC would be covered. I can't see local codes with my tools, and you or the city code office would have to check.
- **Your lease.** It says nothing about AC or repairs. Nothing in it adds a duty or removes one.
- **Which way it cuts.** If a local code requires cooling, the landlord likely has to fix it. If none does, the statute alone may not require it.

**Your formal option**
- **What it does.** Under § 83.56(1), if the landlord materially fails to comply with § 83.51(1) within 7 days after you deliver written notice, you may terminate the lease. The notice must describe the problem and say you intend to terminate because of it.
- **If it's beyond his control.** If the delay is outside his control and he is making every reasonable effort, the statute handles it differently. You could pay reduced rent if you stay. If the unit is untenantable and you leave, you owe no rent while it stays that way (§ 83.56(1)(a)–(b)).
- **Your texts probably aren't enough.** Lease § 7 requires notices to the landlord to be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or sent there "by certified mail." Section 8 says the parties haven't agreed to e-mail notices, and the same section is silent on texts. Section 83.56(4) says notice requirements can't be waived in the lease. A text most likely wouldn't start the 7 days.
- **Next step.** If you want to use this option, send the written notice by hand or certified mail to that office address.

Have you sent the landlord anything besides texts, such as a letter handed to the office or sent by certified mail?

answer:
**Short answer:** Your manager is partly right. You have no automatic right to leave early, but "rent through July no matter what" is not the whole picture.

**What your lease says.** I read the whole lease. Section 3 sets the term as August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026. Nothing in it lets you end early, and nothing sets an early termination fee. Section 10 says the lease can be changed only in a writing signed by both of you. The lease also has no separate early-termination addendum. Under Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4), a fee or liquidated damages is available only if you signed that kind of addendum. So the landlord can't charge a flat fee. A transfer to another school doesn't release you from the lease on its own.

**What the statute gives the landlord if you leave anyway.** Section 83.595 applies once you surrender or abandon the unit. The landlord then has to choose one of these:
- **§ 83.595(1):** Treat the lease as ended and retake possession. Your liability for further rent ends.
- **§ 83.595(2):** Retake possession for your account and re-rent the unit. You owe only the difference between your rent and what the landlord gets from the new tenant. The landlord must try in good faith to re-rent, and any rent received from a new tenant reduces what you owe.
- **§ 83.595(3):** "Stand by and do nothing," and hold you liable for the rent as it comes due. That is the position your manager described.

So if you move out May 15, you could owe rent through July. The landlord can take that route under subsection (3). The landlord can't be forced to take it, though, and the choice is theirs. Rent for May 15 to July 31 would be about 2.5 months at $1,050, but I haven't calculated it.

**What is still open.** I don't know which option the landlord would pick after you leave. The manager's email points to subsection (3). The other reading is that the landlord has to choose, and if they re-rent under subsection (2), your debt shrinks. I also haven't pulled § 83.682, which the search showed allows early termination in some circumstances. Nothing you've told me suggests it applies to you.

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
